title: Emil and the Detectives
author: Erich Kästner
short_summary: Young Emil Tischbein travels alone by train to Berlin carrying money his mother has saved, pinned carefully inside his jacket — and wakes from a doze to find it gone, along with the man who had shared his compartment. Too afraid of the police to report it, Emil follows the thief into the city alone, and is taken up by a crowd of Berlin children who organise themselves into a detective force to hunt the man down.
extended_summary:
Emil's mother is a hairdresser who has saved 140 marks for her own mother in Berlin. Emil, travelling alone for the first time, pins the notes to the lining of his jacket with a sewing needle so that nothing can happen to them. In the compartment a man calling himself Grundeis offers him chocolate; Emil falls asleep, and when he wakes both the man and the money are gone.

Emil does not go to the police. Back in Neustadt he had painted the nose of a monument red, and a policeman had seen him do it, so he feels like something of a criminal himself. Instead he gets off the train early, on the thief's heels, and finds himself alone in Berlin. A boy called Gustav offers to help, fetches a crowd of other children, and within an hour Emil has messengers, lookouts, a collection of pocket money and a plan.

The children shadow Grundeis across the city while Emil's cousin Pony Hütchen keeps the family end going. When the thief tries to change the stolen notes at a bank, Emil proves the money is his by describing the holes the needle left in the paper — a detail only the owner could know. Grundeis turns out to be wanted as a member of a gang of bank robbers, and Emil receives a reward of a thousand marks. His grandmother has the last word: never send money in an envelope — send it by post office order.

questions.prompt: Emil is afraid of losing the money on the journey. What does he do to keep it safe?

options: Pins the notes inside his jacket with a needle
Hides the notes in the lining of his suitcase
Asks the guard to look after them for him
Puts the notes into his shoe under the sock

questions.explanation: It is the most ordinary precaution in the world, and it is what solves the whole case. Kästner plants the needle in chapter two and does not touch it again until the bank at the end — which is exactly how a detective story is supposed to work.

questions.prompt: Emil has just been robbed, but he refuses to go to the police. Why?

options: He had painted a monument's nose red back home
He cannot describe the thief well enough to help
His mother had told him never to speak to police
He has lost his ticket and is afraid of being fined

questions.explanation: A policeman in Neustadt had seen him do it, and ever since, Emil has felt a bit of a criminal himself. It is a child's logic and Kästner takes it perfectly seriously — the whole plot exists because a boy is too embarrassed to ask an adult for help.

questions.prompt: The man who shares Emil's compartment, offers him chocolate and then disappears with the money calls himself ___.
questions.explanation: He gives the name himself, and it is as false as everything else about him. The children track him by his bowler hat rather than by his name, which turns out to be the more reliable of the two.

questions.prompt: At the bank, how does Emil prove that the notes the man is trying to change belong to him?

options: By describing the needle holes in the paper
By reciting the serial numbers of the notes
By showing the empty pocket of his jacket
By producing a receipt from his mother

questions.explanation: Nobody but the owner would know that those particular notes have pin holes in them. The proof is invisible until Emil names it in advance — which is the moment a boy with no money and no adults on his side wins the argument.

questions.prompt: Put the events of Emil's day in the order they happen.

items: Emil's mother gives him the money she has saved
A man in the compartment offers Emil chocolate
Emil wakes and finds his pocket empty
Emil leaves the train early, following the man
Gustav fetches a crowd of Berlin children
The needle holes are described at the bank

questions.explanation: The whole book takes place over roughly a day and a night. Notice how quickly Emil stops being alone: he is by himself in a strange city for only a few pages before a boy he has never met starts organising on his behalf.

questions.prompt: Match each person to their part in the story.

right: Shares a compartment and offers chocolate
The Berlin boy who first offers to help
The cousin who brings the police to the scene
Has the last word about how to send money

questions.explanation: Kästner is careful to let the adults be almost useless until the very end. The people who actually solve this are a boy from a small town, a boy from Berlin, a girl on the family side and, finally, a grandmother with a piece of practical advice.

questions.prompt: Sort each moment by where in the story it belongs.

options.label: Money is pinned into a jacket lining
A stranger hands over a piece of chocolate
A boy falls asleep in a railway compartment
Children collect their pocket money into a fund
A crowd of boys shadows a man through the streets
A man at a counter is asked about pin holes

questions.explanation: The book divides cleanly in two: everything on the left happens to Emil, and everything on the right is something Emil and the others do. The theft is the hinge, and after it he is never passive again.

questions.prompt: Why does the needle matter so much to the way this story works?

options: A careful habit becomes the only evidence there is
It shows that Emil suspected the thief in advance
It is how the children recognise the right man
It proves the thief had been on that train before

questions.explanation: Emil pins the money because he is a careful boy, not because he expects to be robbed. Hundreds of pages later that same small habit is the only thing standing between him and a thief who could otherwise simply say the money was his.

questions.prompt: Emil has just been robbed of money his mother worked hard for, and he decides not to tell the police because of something he once did to a monument. Was he right to keep it to himself and handle it on his own? Give your reasons.
questions.explanation: Both sides can earn full marks. A strong 'he was wrong' answer notices that the money was not his to risk, that the police could have caught the man in an hour, and that his reason was embarrassment rather than sense. A strong 'he was right' answer notices that it worked, that he would not have been believed without proof, and that the children did the job better than a report would have. Accept either, argued from the book.

questions.prompt: The children follow Grundeis across a huge city for hours without him realising. Imagine you had to follow somebody through a busy place without being noticed. Describe two things you would organise in advance and why each one would help.
questions.explanation: There is no single right answer. A strong answer gives two concrete arrangements — taking turns, a place to meet, someone kept by a telephone, a way of passing messages, pooled money for fares — and says what problem each one solves. Naming two things with no reasons is a thinner answer.

questions.prompt: Emil's grandmother has the last word of the book: money should never be sent in an envelope, but always by ___ order.
questions.explanation: After a chase across Berlin, a gang of child detectives and a captured bank robber, the book ends on a piece of household advice. That joke is Kästner all over: the adventure was enormous, and it began because nobody followed a very dull rule.

questions.prompt: When Grundeis is finally caught, what do the children learn about him?

options: He is wanted as one of a gang of bank robbers
He had stolen from children on that line before
He is a hotel porter who had lost his position
He is the brother of one of the Berlin boys

questions.explanation: The man who took a schoolboy's 140 marks turns out to be wanted for a great deal more, which is why the reward is a thousand. Emil's small private disaster has been part of a much bigger case all along, and nobody — including him — knew it.
